newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Britain's Rifkind in Israel to push peace.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Rifkind in Israel to push peace.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind arrived in Israel on Sunday for a visit designed to put pressure on Israel to prove its commitment to the stalled Middle East peace process.
Rifkind will visit the West Bank city of Hebron, aiming to drive home Britain's insistence that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu start taking initiatives to rescue a deteriorating situation.
The visit, sandwiched between talks with Netanyahu, Israeli President Ezer Weizman and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, was cleared with his Israeli hosts, British officials said.

But his insistence on visiting the city still occupied by Israeli troops -- despite an agreement to hand it over to the Palestinians in March -- is a clear message to Netanyahu that Britain wants to see Israel implement peace deals signed by the previous Labour-led government.

Britain sees the delayed redeployment of troops from Hebron, first postponed after a wave of Moslem militant suicide bombings and put on hold again after Netanyahu's election in May, as one of the key reasons for the build-up of Palestinian frustration at the slow progress towards peace.

The frustration erupted in violence after Netanyahu, in what he called an expression of Jewish sovereignty over all of the holy city, opened an archaeological tunnel near Moslem shrines in Jerusalem in September.
In the bloodiest Israeli-Palestinian violence since a framework peace deal was sealed in 1993 by Netanyahu's assassinated predecessor, Yitzhak Rabin, 60 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed.
"One can't assume one can simply delay matters indefinitely without quite a heavy price to be paid," Rifkind said in an Israel Radio interview broadcast on Sunday.

"Sadly the deterioration of the peace process meant that when the tunnel controversy erupted, it led to serious loss of life and that is an important indicator of the dangers which exist," he said in the pre-recorded interview from London.
Diplomats believe a deal is now close to being done on Hebron, leaving the way open for talks on implementing further details of the peace deal.

Rifkind is determined to keep up the pressure, even though there is a risk his visit to Hebron will inflame hardline Jewish settlers in the West Bank. British diplomats said on Sunday they expected the visit to go smoothly although they were ready to change plans if there was any hint of disturbances.
The city, where 400 Jews live in the heart of 100,000 Arabs, is a flashpoint of violence.

British diplomats steadfastly denied there was any intention of Rifkind trying to rival French President Jacques Chirac, who was given a hero's welcome by Palestinians after he publicly turned on Israeli security men and accused them of provocation during a visit to Jerusalem's Old City a week ago.
Rifkind has been careful to avoid criticism of Chirac's visit and France's desire for a greater role in the U.S.-led peace process.
But privately, London -- which wants Europe to complement rather than try to supplant the mediation efforts of the United States -- is wary of Chirac's diplomatic intentions.

In a coded comment, Rifkind told a news conference a week ago: "I don't think anyone in the region, either the Arab countries or the Isralis, wish Europe to get into some sort of competition with the United States for influence."
And on Sunday, officials stressed Rifkind was determined to avoid "megaphone diplomacy" or "grandstanding" -- a word used by British newspaper commentators to describe Chirac's behaviour.
Rifkind flew into Israel from Vietnam after accompanying Queen Elizabeth on a vist to Thailand. He leaves on Monday for Abu Dhabi.
